client: I've been feeling completely stretched thin lately, like no matter what I do, I'm failing at everything. I'm a nurse, so my shifts are already exhausting, and then I come home to my two kids who need me, and my partner is deployed so there's no one to share any of it with. I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to change anything, because the situation is just what it is, you know?
therapist: What you're carrying right now is genuinely enormous — the weight of a demanding job, solo parenting, and missing your partner, all at once — and it makes complete sense that you'd feel stretched to your limit. I also notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's something quiet and almost resigned in the way you're expressing it, like part of you has already had to make peace with just enduring it. I'm curious — when you say talking won't change anything, do you mean you've already tried reaching out before and it didn't help, or does it feel more like you've had to stay so strong for so long that hoping for relief almost feels unsafe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's more the second thing you said — hoping for relief feels almost dangerous, like if I let myself believe things could get easier, I'll fall apart when they don't. I've been holding everything together for so long that I don't even know how to want things to be different anymore. It's like I've just... accepted that this is what my life is now, and that's the only way I can keep going.
therapist: That kind of protective numbness — where you stop letting yourself want things — makes so much sense as a survival strategy when you've had to be the one holding everything together with no end in sight. But I'm struck by something: even the way you're describing this acceptance, there's a kind of exhaustion underneath it, like it costs you something to keep that hope at arm's length. What do you think it would actually feel like to let yourself want things to be different, even just for a moment in this conversation where it's safe to?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... if I'm honest, even thinking about letting myself want something different right now makes my chest feel tight, like I'm about to do something dangerous. It's easier to just say "this is how it is" because the moment I start hoping things could be different, I have to face how much I've actually lost by being the one who holds everything together all the time. And then what do I do with that?
therapist: What you just named is really profound — that hoping means grieving, and grieving means feeling the full weight of what it's cost you to be this strong for this long. That's not a small thing to face, and it makes complete sense that your body braces against it like it's a threat. I want to gently stay with your question though — "what do I do with that?" — because I think part of you is already answering it by being here and saying it out loud; what feels most scary about actually sitting with that grief, even briefly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what scares me most is that if I actually let myself feel it, I won't be able to stop. Like, I've held it together for so long that I genuinely don't trust that there's a bottom to it — that it won't just swallow me whole and I'll fall apart in a way I can't come back from. And I have people depending on me, so I can't afford to do that.
therapist: That fear of there being no bottom — that's one of the loneliest feelings there is, and it speaks to just how long you've been carrying this without anyone to catch you if you stumbled. What I'd gently offer is that the grief doesn't actually work the way that fear tells you it will — feelings, even overwhelming ones, do have a bottom, and falling apart and coming back are not mutually exclusive. I'm wondering, in all this time of holding everyone else together, has there ever been even one person or moment where you let yourself be held a little, and what was that like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I want to say no, that there's never been anyone, but that's not completely true — there was this one time, maybe three years ago, when my friend Dara just sat with me while I cried after my dad got his diagnosis, and she didn't try to fix anything, she just stayed. But even then I remember feeling this pull to apologize for falling apart, like I was being a burden, and I ended up making her tea and asking about her life before the hour was even up. It's like I couldn't let myself stay in that space of being held for more than a few minutes before the guilt kicked in and I had to go back to being the one who holds.
therapist: That moment with Dara sounds like it was genuinely nourishing, even if you could only let yourself have it briefly — and it's so telling that your instinct was to make her tea, to immediately restore the balance by becoming the caregiver again the moment you'd taken up any space. That guilt you felt, the sense of being a burden just for crying with a friend who chose to be there — I'm curious where you think that belief came from, that your needs are something other people have to be protected from rather than something you're allowed to have?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... when you put it like that, it does sound kind of automatic, doesn't it — the tea thing. Like I didn't even decide to do it, I just got up and started doing it. I think it probably goes back pretty far, honestly, maybe to when my mom was going through her depression and I learned really early that the way to keep things okay was to not add to what she was already carrying.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that little girl learned to make herself small and take care of others not because she wanted to, but because it felt like the only way to keep things safe, and that lesson has been running quietly in the background ever since. The way you're speaking about it right now, there's something very soft and almost far-away in your voice, like you're touching something tender and old. I want to ask gently — what do you feel toward that little girl who taught herself to make tea instead of taking up space?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I feel... sad for her, honestly. Like, she was just trying to hold everything together, and nobody even noticed how much that cost her. But I also feel a little strange saying that, like I'm being dramatic or making it bigger than it was.
therapist: The sadness you just named for her is real and it's not dramatic — a child quietly learning to disappear her own needs to keep the peace is genuinely something worth grieving. But I notice that even as you said it, there was something that sounded almost muted, like the feeling was there but you were holding it at a careful distance, which makes me wonder if that same voice that calls it "dramatic" is the same one that made you get up and make Dara tea. What would it mean about you if what that little girl went through actually was as significant as it feels right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it would mean that I wasn't just being oversensitive all those years, that the way I felt small and invisible actually had a reason behind it. And that's... I don't know, it's almost harder to sit with than just thinking I was too much, because if it was real then I have to figure out what to do with that. I guess part of me is afraid that if I actually let it matter, I'll just fall apart and there won't be anyone there to help me put things back together.
therapist: What you just said — that it's harder to believe you were valid than to keep blaming yourself — is one of the most honest and courageous things you could have named, and it makes complete sense that it feels destabilizing. And I want to gently push back on that fear of falling apart alone, because you're actually doing something really important right now — you're letting it matter, here, in this space, and you haven't fallen apart, you've gone deeper. What if allowing it to be real doesn't have to mean doing that alone — what would it feel like to let this space, and me, be a small part of that net?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to hold onto that... the idea that this space could be part of something that holds me. But there's this other part that keeps reminding me that sessions end, that you have other clients, that this isn't... permanent, I guess. It feels risky to let myself lean on something that has a clock on it, because what happens when I walk out that door and it's just me again?
therapist: That fear is so understandable, and it actually reflects something really important — you've learned that relying on things that don't last is how you get hurt, so of course part of you wants to protect yourself from that. But I want to gently offer a different way of seeing it: the goal here isn't to replace that aloneness with me, it's to help you build something inside yourself that comes with you when you walk out that door — a different relationship with your own needs, your own grief, your own worthiness of care. What if the work we do here isn't something that ends when the session does, but something that slowly becomes yours to keep?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That sounds really beautiful when you say it like that, but honestly, I'm not sure I fully believe it yet. Like, I want to — I really do — but every time I've tried to hold onto something good, it just kind of slips away, and I'm left feeling more empty than before. How do I know this time will be any different, that I won't just walk out of here and feel just as alone as I did when I walked in?
therapist: That question deserves an honest answer, and I won't promise you that you'll walk out feeling completely different — but I did notice something just now: even in the middle of that doubt, you said "I want to believe it, I really do," and that wanting is not nothing. The fact that you're asking "how do I know it will be different" rather than "I know it won't be" tells me there's a part of you still reaching, still hoping, even after everything that's taught you not to. What if we made that the starting point — not certainty, but just that small, stubborn part of you that showed up today anyway?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
